17.text:
Tourism is one of the world's largest industries, and many countries try to attract more visitors. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on tourism: economic gains and a stronger sense of cultural pride.

First and foremost, tourism brings income, jobs and foreign currency to the host country. Visitors spend money on hotels, food, transport and souvenirs, which supports many small businesses, and the roads, airports and services built for tourists also benefit residents. A family that opens a small guesthouse, for example, earns a living and also buys food and services from neighbours, so the money spreads through the community. Tourism creates jobs for people with a wide range of skills, from guides and drivers to cooks and cleaners, and it can reach regions where other industries are weak. Foreign currency earned from visitors can pay for imports and help the national economy.

In addition, tourism strengthens cultural pride and understanding. When visitors show interest in local traditions, music, food and history, residents have a reason to preserve them, and crafts that might have disappeared can survive because tourists want to buy them. Contact with people from other countries also broadens horizons, encourages language learning and can reduce prejudice on both sides. Historic buildings and parks that would be too expensive to maintain from local taxes alone can be protected using entrance fees. Although tourism needs careful management so that it does not damage the places it depends on, a country that plans well can enjoy lasting benefits.

To sum up, tourism brings clear benefits to a country, above all income and employment and a stronger sense of cultural identity. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

30.text:
In some countries, beaches and historic cities attract millions of visitors every year, and some argue that tourism is the main reason for economic growth. I disagree to a large extent, since tourism is important for some economies but cannot explain growth in most countries, where industry, services and technology matter more.

To begin with, tourism does bring income, jobs and foreign currency to the host country. Visitors spend money on hotels, food, transport and souvenirs, which supports many small businesses, and for small islands with few other resources it can indeed be the largest source of income. A family that opens a small guesthouse, for example, earns a living and also buys food and services from neighbours. In such places, tourism is a central part of growth, and its loss would be severe.

However, for most countries tourism is not the main driver of growth. Large economies such as Germany, Japan and South Korea grew mainly through manufacturing, trade, education and technology, not through visitors. Moreover, dependence on tourism makes an economy fragile. Income rises and falls with the seasons and with events such as disease or recession, crowds strain water and roads, and much of the profit may go to foreign hotel chains. A small island that relies on tourism, for instance, can lose most of its income in a single year if flights are cancelled. Many tourism jobs are also seasonal and low-paid. A balanced economy, with agriculture, industry and services, is safer and brings more stable growth.

In conclusion, tourism contributes to economic growth in some places, but it is rarely the main reason, so I disagree with the statement to a large extent.

128.text:
Many villages and small towns in the countryside are turning to tourism as farming and traditional industries decline. This essay will discuss the main advantages and disadvantages of tourism for rural areas before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, tourism can give rural communities a new source of income. Farm stays, guided walks and craft sales create jobs where few exist and encourage young people to stay, which slows the decline of villages. A village that offers farm stays, for example, can keep young people from leaving to find work in cities. Visitors also buy local food and handmade goods, so traditional skills and products gain a market, and money spent in the countryside tends to stay there if owners are local. The investment in roads, internet and services that tourism brings also improves daily life for residents.

On the negative side, however, tourism has real drawbacks. The work is often seasonal and low-paid, prices for housing and food may rise so that local people struggle to afford them, and outside investors may take the profits. Crowds, traffic and noise can spoil the peaceful character that attracted visitors in the first place, and traditional ways of life may be turned into a show for tourists. Nevertheless, these problems can be reduced. Benefits are greatest when the community owns and controls the businesses, when numbers of visitors are limited and when regulations protect the landscape and local housing.

In conclusion, tourism offers rural areas valuable income and jobs, but it can bring pressure on prices and traditions. On balance, I believe that it is beneficial when it is small in scale, locally owned and carefully managed.

Việc làm theo mùa lương thấp; giá nhà và thực phẩm tăng; nhà đầu tư ngoài lấy lợi nhuận; đông, tắc đường, ồn phá không khí yên bình; lối sống truyền thống thành trò diễn. Nevertheless: cộng đồng sở hữu và kiểm soát, giới hạn lượng khách, quy định bảo vệ cảnh quan và nhà ở.

190.text:
Cities and towns around the world hold music, food, lantern and religious festivals, and some argue that cultural festivals boost tourism. I largely agree, since a well-known festival gives visitors a clear reason to travel, although the effect depends on how well it is organised.

To begin with, festivals give visitors a clear reason to travel and to spend money. A well-known music, food or cultural festival attracts people from other regions and countries, often outside the main holiday season, and fills hotels, restaurants and shops. A lantern festival held in the quiet winter months, for example, can fill hotels that would otherwise be empty. Visitors often stay several days and spend on transport, food and gifts, so local businesses benefit widely. Festivals also provide ready-made material for photographs, videos and social media, which spreads the name of the destination far beyond its own borders at very low cost.

Furthermore, festivals shape the image of a place and encourage repeat visits. A town that becomes famous for a distinctive celebration is remembered as lively and welcoming, and many visitors return, sometimes outside the festival dates, to explore further. However, the effect is not guaranteed. Festivals are temporary, and tourism in the rest of the year may stay weak if the town has little else to offer. Overcrowding, noise and rubbish can upset residents, and a poorly organised or badly advertised festival may attract few people. Authorities should therefore plan transport, safety and cleaning carefully, involve local people and combine festivals with other attractions throughout the year.

In conclusion, cultural festivals boost tourism to a large extent by attracting visitors and publicity, provided that they are well run and supported by year-round attractions.

310.text:
Rainforests, coral reefs, mountains and polar regions attract adventurous travellers, but these ecosystems recover slowly from damage. This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of encouraging tourism in fragile ecosystems before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, tourism in fragile ecosystems can fund their protection. Entrance fees and local jobs give people a reason to protect wildlife instead of hunting or clearing land, and visitors who see these places in person often become supporters of conservation. A national park that charges visitors, for example, can pay rangers and research that would otherwise be unaffordable. Guides, boat operators and lodge workers earn a living from nature that is kept intact, which reduces pressure from poaching and logging. Tourism also raises international awareness, which can attract donations and political support.

On the negative side, however, tourism can damage the places that visitors come to admire. Trampling, litter, noise and introduced species can harm habitats that recover slowly, and wildlife may change its behaviour or leave when disturbed. Divers who touch a coral reef, for example, can destroy in a moment what took decades to grow. Hotels, roads and airports built for visitors cause further harm, and flights add greenhouse gas emissions. Nevertheless, these risks can be managed through strict limits on visitor numbers and behaviour, permits, trained guides, zoning of sensitive areas and the use of fees to fund monitoring. Where such controls are absent, tourism should not be encouraged.

In conclusion, tourism can pay for the protection of fragile ecosystems, but it can also destroy them. On balance, I believe that it should be encouraged only in small numbers, under strict control, and where the income supports conservation.

analysis.type_vi: A/D: khuyến khích du lịch ở hệ sinh thái mong manh

plan.think: Mở bài nêu các hệ sinh thái (rừng mưa, rạn san hô, núi, vùng cực) và đặc điểm hồi phục chậm; kết luận chọn lập trường có điều kiện.

Phí vào cửa và việc làm địa phương cho người dân lý do bảo vệ thay vì săn bắn, phá đất; du khách trở thành người ủng hộ bảo tồn; vườn quốc gia thu phí trả cho kiểm lâm, nghiên cứu; nâng nhận thức quốc tế.

Giẫm đạp, rác, tiếng ồn, loài ngoại lai hại môi trường sống hồi phục chậm; động vật thay đổi hành vi hoặc bỏ đi. Ví dụ thợ lặn chạm rạn san hô phá cái mất hàng chục năm để lớn. Khách sạn, đường, sân bay và chuyến bay thêm khí thải. Nevertheless: giới hạn số khách, giấy phép, hướng dẫn viên, phân vùng, phí cho giám sát.
Chỉ khuyến khích với số lượng nhỏ, kiểm soát chặt, thu nhập phục vụ bảo tồn.

320.text:
Some travellers book flights and hotels on their own and go wherever they please, while others join organised group tours. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of solo travel argue that it offers freedom, flexibility and personal growth. Travellers choose their own route and pace, stay longer where they feel happy and leave places they dislike, and they meet local people more easily because they are not part of a crowd. A solo traveller who changes plans to follow a local's recommendation, for example, may discover a village that no tour would visit. Solving problems alone, from reading maps to bargaining for a bed, builds confidence and independence, and many people return from such journeys more mature. Travelling alone can also be cheaper if one chooses simple food and transport.

On the other hand, supporters of group tours point out that they are convenient, safe and good value. Transport, hotels and guides are organised in advance, costs are shared, and a knowledgeable guide explains the history of each place. A group visiting an ancient temple with a trained guide, for example, learns far more than someone reading a brief sign. Group tours are especially suitable for first-time travellers, older people and those who do not speak the local language, because help is always at hand. Friendships formed on the trip can also be rewarding. However, the schedule is fixed and contact with local life may be limited.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I prefer to travel alone or with a small group of friends in familiar places, but I would choose a guided tour for remote or unfamiliar regions where safety and language are concerns.

analysis.type_vi: Discuss both views: du lịch một mình hay đi tour đoàn

Tự do, linh hoạt, trưởng thành: chọn lộ trình và nhịp độ; ở lâu nơi thích; gặp người địa phương dễ hơn; tự giải quyết vấn đề xây dựng tự tin; có thể rẻ hơn. Ví dụ du khách đổi kế hoạch theo gợi ý của người địa phương phát hiện ngôi làng không tour nào đến.

Tiện, an toàn, giá trị tốt: vận chuyển, khách sạn, hướng dẫn viên sắp sẵn; chia chi phí; hướng dẫn viên giải thích lịch sử. Ví dụ nhóm thăm đền cổ có hướng dẫn viên. Hợp người đi lần đầu, người lớn tuổi, không biết ngôn ngữ. Giới hạn: lịch trình cố định, ít tiếp xúc cuộc sống địa phương.
Tự đi hoặc nhóm nhỏ nơi quen thuộc; chọn tour có hướng dẫn cho vùng xa lạ cần an toàn và ngôn ngữ.

404.text:
Millions of people now travel for pleasure, and popular destinations suffer from litter, crowds, rising prices and damage to nature. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on limiting the impact of visitors and on keeping the benefits in local communities.

To begin with, governments should limit the impact of visitors on popular sites. Visitor caps and environmental fees protect fragile places, rules on waste and water reduce pollution, and strict building regulations prevent hotels from destroying coastlines and forests. A famous trail that issues only a fixed number of daily permits, for example, stays in good condition while still welcoming visitors. Public transport and walking routes can replace cars in crowded areas, and tourist taxes can pay for cleaning, repairs and conservation. Information at airports and hotels can explain local rules, such as not feeding animals or touching coral.

In addition, authorities should make sure that tourism benefits local people and respects their culture. Certification schemes and loans for small, locally owned guesthouses and tour operators keep more income in the community, while training helps residents to work as guides and managers instead of low-paid staff. Governments can also require consultation with villages before new developments are approved, and support the preservation of local crafts and traditions. Equally important, campaigns can encourage visitors to choose responsible operators and to behave respectfully, for example by dressing appropriately at sacred sites. These measures cost little compared with the long-term damage caused by uncontrolled tourism, and they protect the places that visitors come to see.

In conclusion, limiting the impact of visitors and keeping the benefits local offer the most realistic way of fostering responsible tourism.

407.text:
A few private companies now offer short trips beyond the atmosphere to those who can pay, and some people believe that space tourism will benefit humanity. Others disagree. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that space tourism may drive new technology and inspire people. Competition between companies can lower the cost of rockets, and developments in materials, engines and life-support systems often find uses on Earth, as earlier space programmes did. The sight of ordinary people travelling to orbit may also encourage young people to study science and engineering, and astronauts who see the planet from space often describe a stronger sense of its fragility and unity. A company that learns to reuse rockets, for example, may make future satellite launches cheaper, which benefits communication and weather forecasting. Over time, space tourism might even help to develop research facilities in orbit.

On the other hand, critics point out that its benefits to humanity are uncertain. Flights are affordable only to the very rich, release significant emissions and carry real risks, and the same money and talent could be used on problems such as poverty, disease and climate change. Public attention and funding may also be diverted from more useful space science, such as monitoring the Earth. A flight that costs as much as a hospital ward, for instance, seems a poor use of resources when many people lack basic care. Supporters of the industry may exaggerate its social value to attract investors.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that space tourism is mainly an entertainment for the wealthy, and that its benefits to humanity will be limited unless emissions are controlled and the technology serves wider scientific goals.

analysis.type_vi: Discuss both views: du lịch vũ trụ có đem lại lợi ích cho nhân loại không

plan.think: Mở bài mô tả hiện trạng (vài công ty tư nhân bán chuyến ngắn ra ngoài khí quyển); mỗi thân bài một phía; ý kiến riêng thiên về hoài nghi có điều kiện.

Cạnh tranh giảm chi phí tên lửa; vật liệu, động cơ, hệ thống hỗ trợ sự sống có ứng dụng trên Trái Đất; truyền cảm hứng người trẻ học khoa học; phi hành gia thấy hành tinh mong manh. Ví dụ công ty học tái sử dụng tên lửa làm phóng vệ tinh rẻ hơn.

Chỉ người rất giàu mua nổi, phát thải đáng kể, rủi ro; tiền và nhân tài có thể dùng cho nghèo đói, bệnh tật, khí hậu; sự chú ý có thể chệch khỏi khoa học vũ trụ hữu ích hơn. Ví dụ chuyến bay đắt bằng một khoa bệnh viện.
Chủ yếu là giải trí cho người giàu; lợi ích hạn chế trừ khi kiểm soát phát thải và phục vụ mục tiêu khoa học rộng hơn.

420.text:
Travellers today can cross a continent by high-speed train or fly across an ocean in a few hours, and opinions differ on which is the better way to travel. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of train travel point to comfort, convenience and environmental benefits. Trains produce far fewer emissions per passenger, run from city centre to city centre and offer space, comfort and scenery. A traveller who takes a train between two capital cities four hours apart, for example, arrives in the centre, rested, without airport queues, security checks and long journeys to distant terminals. Passengers can work, read or sleep on board, and stations are often close to restaurants and hotels. For journeys up to about five hours, trains can be as quick as planes when travel to the airport and waiting time are included, and they are less affected by weather.

On the other hand, supporters of air travel emphasise speed and reach. Planes cut hours from long journeys and connect places that no railway could, such as islands and continents divided by oceans. For a trip of several thousand kilometres, flying is the only realistic option for most people, and low-cost airlines have made it cheaper than many train tickets. Business travellers who must attend a meeting overseas, for instance, cannot afford to spend two days on trains. However, flying causes pollution, noise and stress at airports, and flight delays are common.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that trains are the better choice for short and medium distances, because they are cleaner and more pleasant, while planes remain necessary for long journeys across oceans.

analysis.type_vi: Discuss both views: đi tàu hoả hay máy bay

plan.think: Mở bài nêu hai khả năng (tàu cao tốc băng qua lục địa / máy bay vượt đại dương trong vài giờ); mỗi thân bài một phía; ý kiến riêng theo khoảng cách.

Thoải mái, tiện, thân thiện môi trường: phát thải mỗi hành khách ít hơn nhiều, từ trung tâm đến trung tâm; ví dụ hành khách giữa hai thủ đô cách bốn giờ đến trung tâm, nghỉ ngơi, không xếp hàng sân bay; làm việc, đọc, ngủ; với chặng đến khoảng năm giờ tàu có thể nhanh ngang máy bay, ít bị thời tiết.

Tốc độ và tầm với: rút ngắn hàng giờ, nối nơi tàu không tới (đảo, lục địa cách đại dương); hãng giá rẻ rẻ hơn nhiều vé tàu; ví dụ doanh nhân họp ở nước ngoài không thể mất hai ngày. Giới hạn: ô nhiễm, ồn, căng thẳng sân bay, hoãn chuyến.
Tàu cho chặng ngắn và vừa vì sạch và dễ chịu hơn; máy bay cần thiết cho chặng dài qua đại dương.

425.text:
Cities such as Edinburgh, Avignon and Salzburg are known worldwide for their arts festivals, and music, theatre and visual arts events have become a significant part of the tourism industry. This essay will outline two key roles that arts festivals play in promoting tourism: attracting visitors and spending, and building a lasting reputation for a place.

First and foremost, arts festivals give visitors a clear reason to travel and to spend money. A well-known music, theatre or arts festival attracts people from other regions and countries, often outside the main holiday season, and fills hotels, restaurants and shops. A lantern festival held in the quiet winter months, for example, can fill hotels that would otherwise be empty, and the same is true of a jazz weekend or a film festival. Visitors usually stay several days and spend on transport, meals and gifts, and the festival creates jobs for performers, technicians, guides and hospitality staff. Local artists also gain an audience and income that they might not find otherwise.

In addition, arts festivals build a lasting reputation. A town that becomes famous for a distinctive celebration is remembered as lively, creative and welcoming, and the publicity from newspapers, television and social media spreads its name at little cost. Many visitors return in other seasons to explore more of the area, and the festival's fame can attract investment and new residents. However, the effect depends on quality and planning. Poorly organised events may disappoint visitors, and crowds can upset residents, so authorities should plan transport, safety and cleaning carefully and combine the festival with year-round attractions.

To sum up, arts festivals promote tourism by drawing visitors and spending and by creating a lasting reputation. For these reasons, they deserve continued public support.

461.text:
Package holidays, cruise ships and budget flights have made travel possible for millions of people, and mass tourism now affects beaches, mountains and old cities worldwide. This essay will discuss the advantages and the environmental damage before explaining whether the advantages outweigh the damage.

On the positive side, mass tourism creates income for millions of people. Hotels, restaurants, transport companies and shops depend on large numbers of visitors, and whole regions would be poor without them. A family that opens a small guesthouse, for example, earns a living and also buys food and services from neighbours. Taxes from tourism pay for roads, airports and public services that residents also use, and falling prices have allowed ordinary families, not just the rich, to see the world and learn about other cultures. For many developing countries, tourism is one of the few industries that can bring rapid growth.

On the negative side, however, mass tourism can harm the environment on a large scale. Crowds produce litter, emissions and heavy water use, and coastlines and wildlife suffer. A resort built directly on a beach, for example, can damage dunes and turtle nests while employing hundreds of local people. Flights add to climate change, and popular sites can be worn down by too many feet. Nevertheless, much of this damage can be reduced. Limits on visitor numbers, strict building rules, better waste treatment and fees for the use of sensitive sites can protect the environment while keeping the income. Without such controls, the damage may eventually destroy the attractions that tourism depends on.

In conclusion, the advantages of mass tourism outweigh the environmental damage only when numbers and building are carefully controlled, and governments must ensure that this is done.

analysis.type_vi: A/D: lợi thế của du lịch đại trà có lớn hơn thiệt hại môi trường không — chỉ khi được kiểm soát

plan.think: Phán quyết có điều kiện: lợi thế lớn hơn chỉ khi kiểm soát số lượng và xây dựng. Thân bài 2 dùng Nevertheless để đề xuất giải pháp.

Thu nhập cho hàng triệu người; khách sạn, nhà hàng, vận tải, cửa hàng phụ thuộc đông khách; thuế trả đường, sân bay, dịch vụ công; giá giảm cho phép người bình thường đi du lịch và hiểu văn hoá khác; ngành tăng trưởng nhanh ở nước đang phát triển. Ví dụ gia đình mở nhà nghỉ nhỏ.

Đám đông gây rác, khí thải, dùng nhiều nước; bờ biển và động vật chịu thiệt; chuyến bay thêm biến đổi khí hậu. Ví dụ khu nghỉ dưỡng xây trực tiếp trên bãi biển phá đụn cát và tổ rùa nhưng thuê hàng trăm người địa phương. Nevertheless: giới hạn khách, quy định xây dựng, xử lý rác, phí cho khu vực nhạy cảm.
